notes: Slot 0 is the Lithuanian Diplomatic Service under Stasys Lozoraitis (continuity of the Smetona-era state). The exile Christian Democrats (MD slot 14) are placed in slot 1, which has starting popularity and fits Christian democracy; slot 14 holds the Catholic Church. VLIK has no slot of its own but is referenced in the LKDP, LSDP and LVLS texts. Slot 7 is the Lithuanian KGB as 'Saugumas' (chairman Juozas Petkevičius since 1967). Slot 22 is the Riflemen's Union re-founded in exile in Chicago in 1954; slot 23 follows MD with the Urach branch of Württemberg (Mindaugas II). The LIT sprites (TS-LKD, LVŽS) show post-1990 parties, so all icons are null.

0.name: Lietuvos diplomatinė tarnyba
0.text:
The Lithuanian Diplomatic Service is the surviving apparatus of the pre-war Republic. In June 1940, on the eve of the Soviet occupation, the Lithuanian government secretly named Stasys Lozoraitis, envoy in Rome and Antanas Smetona's former foreign minister, Chief of the Diplomatic Service. Lozoraitis has led it from Rome ever since, with legations in Washington and London that Western governments still recognise.

It embodies the legal continuity of the Smetona-era state: non-recognition of the annexation, custody of Lithuanian assets abroad and passports for exiles. Pro-Western and conservative, it claims to stand above émigré parties, which has fuelled a long rivalry with the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania over who speaks for the nation. Its leverage is legal and diplomatic, resting on Washington's policy of non-recognition.

1.name: Lietuvos krikščionių demokratų partija
1.text:
The Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party was the strongest party of the parliamentary republic in the 1920s; it briefly backed Antanas Smetona's 1926 coup before being pushed into opposition and banned in 1936. In exile it is the leading force in the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania, and its patriarch is the priest Mykolas Krupavičius, architect of the land reform and the committee's chairman from 1945 to 1955, now living in Chicago.

It stands for a restored democratic Lithuania built on Catholic social teaching: the family, private property tempered by social justice, Catholic schooling and ties to the Holy See. It distrusts both the Smetona nationalists and the liberals who seek contacts with Soviet Lithuania. Its leverage lies in the parishes, press and associations of Lithuanian America.

2.name: Santara-Šviesa
2.text:
Santara-Šviesa is the federation of liberal Lithuanian exile intellectuals formed in 1957 by the merger of two student movements born in the post-war refugee years. Its leading mind is the sociologist Vytautas Kavolis, editor of the journal Metmenys, and its annual summer conferences in the American Midwest draw scholars, writers and young professionals raised in exile.

It stands for liberal democracy, pluralism, secular culture and an open, critical debate on Lithuanian history, including the uncomfortable chapters of 1941. Unlike most exile bodies it favours cautious cultural contacts with Soviet Lithuania as a bridge to the people at home, which earns it charges of naivety from the Catholic and nationalist establishment. Its leverage lies in ideas, in American universities and in the younger generation of the emigration.

3.name: Lietuvos socialdemokratų partija
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Lithuania, founded in 1896, is the oldest Lithuanian political party. A partner in the 1926 coalition overthrown by Smetona's coup and banned with the other parties in 1936, it reconstituted itself in exile, where it sits in the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania and belongs to the Socialist International. Its long-time leader Steponas Kairys, a signatory of the 1918 Act of Independence, died in New York in 1964.

It stands for a restored parliamentary democracy with a welfare state, trade-union rights and secular education. It rejects Soviet rule as a perversion of socialism and works with Western social democrats to keep Baltic independence on the agenda. Its base is ageing pre-war activists in America and Western Europe.

4.name: Lietuvos komunistų partija
4.text:
The Communist Party of Lithuania is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party of the Lithuanian SSR. Founded in 1918 and illegal throughout independence, it was carried to power by the Soviet annexation of 1940 and led through the war against the partisans by Antanas Sniečkus, its First Secretary since 1936 and now among the Union's longest-serving party chiefs.

Sniečkus pairs unwavering loyalty to Moscow with a careful defence of Lithuanian interests: native cadres in leading posts, restrained immigration, new industry spread to provincial towns rather than concentrated in Vilnius, and measured tolerance for national culture. Under him a small underground sect has become a mass party of Lithuanians. It controls every institution of the republic.

5.name: Lietuvos Lenino komunistinė jaunimo sąjunga
5.english: Lenin Communist Youth Union of Lithuania
5.text:
The Lenin Communist Youth Union of Lithuania is the republic's Komsomol, enrolling most young people between fourteen and twenty-eight and serving as the school of future party cadres. In the 1940s its activists fought beside the security forces against the partisans and drove collectivisation in the villages; today it runs youth newspapers, construction brigades, summer camps and civil rites meant to replace church weddings.

It speaks for the militant side of Soviet socialism: atheism, labour heroism, internationalism and contempt for Catholic 'superstition' and bourgeois nationalism. Yet in Kaunas and Vilnius it struggles to hold a generation drawn to Western rock music, long hair and parish youth groups. Its leverage lies in numbers, in its monopoly on youth organisation and in its role as the ladder to party careers.

6.name: Liaudies gynėjai
6.text:
The People's Defenders is the official name of the destroyer battalions that hunted the Lithuanian partisans from 1944 into the early 1950s, men whom villagers still call 'stribai' with contempt. Their veterans now serve as raion officials, militiamen, kolkhoz chairmen, honoured by the regime and resented by neighbours who remember the burnings, arrests and deportations.

They form the hardline backbone of the countryside: hostile to the deportees returning from Siberia, to the Catholic clergy and to any softening of the official verdict on the 'bandits' of the forests. They want ideological vigilance, militant atheism and the post-war struggle kept as the founding myth of Soviet Lithuania. Their leverage lies in rural networks, in their ties to the security organs that once commanded them and in their unquestioned loyalty.

7.name: Saugumas
7.text:
Saugumas, the name of the inter-war Lithuanian security police, is what Lithuanians call the KGB of the Lithuanian SSR, headquartered on Lenin Avenue in Vilnius in the building where the NKVD and MGB once interrogated and executed partisans. Since 1967 it has been led by Juozas Petkevičius, and it answers to Yuri Andropov in Moscow.

As a power bloc it stands for relentless vigilance: penetrating the Catholic clergy and the Kaunas seminary, watching returning deportees, writers and students, and filtering every contact with the large Lithuanian emigration in America. It regards Lithuania as the most restive of the Baltic republics and its church as a hostile organisation. Its leverage lies in a dense web of informers and files on all who matter.

8.name: Odlar Yurdu
8.text:
Land of Fire, a poetic name for Azerbaijan, is the informal circle of the small Azerbaijani community in Lithuania: construction specialists, seamen of the merchant fleet based at Klaipėda, students in Kaunas and former conscripts. There is no Shia mosque or cleric anywhere in the republic, so they meet in each other's homes for Novruz and for quiet Muharram remembrances.

The circle asks only for room to live as Shia Muslims within Soviet law: to gather on holy days, to circumcise their sons and to bury their dead by Islamic rite. It shuns politics, keeps on good terms with managers and the militia and takes its cues from the official Shia clergy in Baku. Its leverage is limited to the mutual support of men far from home.

9.name: Aşura Camaatı
9.text:
The Ashura Congregation gathers the most devout Azerbaijani Shias in Vilnius and Klaipėda, mostly older workers from the villages of the Azerbaijani SSR, who on the tenth day of Muharram mourn the martyrdom of Imam Husayn at Karbala with elegies and private rites. They keep a few hand-copied prayer books and recite from memory what their fathers learned in mosques closed in the 1930s.

They regard the Soviet compromise with religion as a trial imposed by tyrants and the official Spiritual Administration in Baku as a tool of atheists. Their hopes rest with the senior clergy of Najaf and Qom, whom they consider the true guides of the community and whose rulings reach them only by hearsay. Their circle is tiny and secretive, but its fervour is complete.

10.name: Keturiasdešimt Totorių
10.text:
The Forty Tatars takes its name from the old Tatar village near Vilnius whose wooden mosque has served the community for generations, a symbol of the Lithuanian Tatars settled in the Grand Duchy by Vytautas the Great more than five centuries ago. They live around Vilnius and Kaunas and in villages such as Nemėžis and Raižiai, speak Lithuanian, Polish or Russian, and keep their Hanafi faith and the mizar cemeteries of their ancestors.

They practise a loyal, quietist Islam under the distant authority of the Spiritual Administration in Ufa, avoid politics and ask only that their few remaining houses of prayer stay open. Proud of centuries of service to Lithuanian rulers, they enjoy a respect other Muslims in the Union lack. Their leverage is that of an ancient, trusted community.

11.name: Halqat al-Ummah
11.text:
The Ummah Circle is a clandestine study group of a few Arab students at the institutes of Kaunas and Vilnius who came on scholarships for 'progressive' youth but were shaken by the defeat of June 1967 and disillusioned with Nasserism and Marxism alike. In their dormitories they read Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets and the writings of Sayyid Qutb, executed in Cairo in 1966.

They believe the Muslim world can be redeemed only by erasing the borders drawn by colonial powers and restoring a single caliphate under Islamic law, and they see the Soviet Union as another empire of unbelief. They keep apart from the local Tatars, whom they think lax, and fear the informers among their classmates. Their influence is nil beyond their circle, but their conviction is absolute.

12.name: Vytauto mečetė
12.text:
The Vytautas Mosque circle gathers the Tatar families of Kaunas around the brick mosque their community completed in 1933 to mark the five-hundredth anniversary of the death of Vytautas the Great, the proudest monument of Muslim citizenship in inter-war Lithuania. In those years Kaunas Tatars cultivated ties with Turkey and took a visible part in the civic life of the temporary capital.

They uphold a modern, educated Islam in harmony with Lithuanian patriotism: religious instruction for children, community self-organisation, mutual aid and a mosque that is a civic as well as a spiritual centre. Under Soviet rule they keep a low profile, but they hope to revive their associations and restore the mosque's place in public life. Their leverage lies in their reputation as loyal, educated citizens of long standing.

13.name: Lietuvos TSR Ministrų Taryba
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Lithuanian SSR
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Lithuanian SSR is the republic's government, chaired since 1967 by Juozas Maniušis. It directs the republican ministries, the State Planning Committee and the local soviets, and under Sniečkus's protection it has steered new factories toward provincial towns such as Panevėžys and Alytus instead of letting Vilnius swell with migrant labour.

Its engineers and planners, many of them young Lithuanians trained at the Kaunas Polytechnic Institute, favour pragmatic modernisation: Kosygin's cost-accounting reforms, land melioration, housing and consumer goods. They prefer to recruit local labour rather than import it and defend republican budgets against the Union ministries. Their leverage lies in the plan, the budget and the expertise that keeps the republic's rapid industrialisation running.

14.name: Lietuvos Katalikų Bažnyčia
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Lithuania is the faith of the great majority of Lithuanians and the most powerful institution beyond the party's control. It survives under heavy pressure: Bishops Julijonas Steponavičius and Vincentas Sladkevičius have been banished to remote parishes for defying the authorities, the single seminary in Kaunas may admit only a handful of candidates each year, and organised religious teaching of children is a criminal offence.

Its conservatism is national and moral rather than partisan: faith, family and the Lithuanian language. In the last two years priests have begun petitioning Soviet leaders against the seminary quotas and the harassment of believers, a sign of growing defiance. Its leverage lies in its hold on the villages, its moral authority and the attention of the Vatican and Lithuanian America.

15.name: Lietuvių Fondas
15.text:
The Lithuanian Foundation was established in Chicago in 1962 as a permanent endowment of the Lithuanian-American community: members buy shares whose capital is never spent, and only the income goes to schools, culture, scholarship and patriotic causes. Its backers are the physicians, engineers, building contractors and businessmen who have prospered since the post-war refugees reached America.

It is the nearest thing Lithuania has to an organised moneyed elite, and it thinks like one: private property, free enterprise and a future independent Lithuania rebuilt with emigrant capital and know-how. It finances the émigré press, Saturday schools and academic publishing, and its donors carry weight in every exile organisation. Its leverage lies in a growing capital base and in the business networks of Chicago, Cleveland and Los Angeles.

16.name: Vienkiemių žmonės
16.text:
The Homestead People are the Lithuanian farmers who still cling to the vienkiemis, the isolated family farmstead created by the inter-war land reform, which the authorities are now dismantling by moving households into collective-farm settlements under the land melioration programme. Kolkhoz workers by day, they live from their private plots, their cows and orchards, and sell their surplus at city markets.

Their creed is property and independence: the family farm, free markets for produce, low taxes and freedom from the brigadier and the planner. They distrust every authority beyond the parish and remember the land reform of the 1920s as the foundation of a free peasantry. Their leverage lies in private plots that supply much of the republic's meat, milk and vegetables, and in sheer rural stubbornness.

17.name: Lietuvos gamtos apsaugos draugija
17.text:
The Lithuanian Nature Protection Society was founded in Vilnius in 1960 as a voluntary society under official patronage and has grown into one of the republic's largest public organisations, with branches in schools, factories and collective farms. Its scientists and teachers hold conferences, run nature-protection courses at people's universities and organise school competitions.

It campaigns for the forests, lakes and the great dunes of the Curonian Spit, for reserves such as Žuvintas, and against reckless drainage, the pollution of the Nemunas and the drowning of valleys by projects like the Kaunas reservoir. It avoids open politics, yet in defending the native landscape it gives Lithuanians a legal language of national belonging. Its leverage lies in mass membership and the sympathy of writers and scientists.

18.name: Lietuvos valstiečių liaudininkų sąjunga
18.text:
The Lithuanian Popular Peasants' Union was the main centre-left party of independent Lithuania, the party of President Kazys Grinius, whose 1926 coalition government with the Social Democrats was overthrown by Smetona's coup. Banned with the other parties in 1936, it reconstituted itself in exile as a member of the Supreme Committee for the Liberation of Lithuania; Grinius himself died in Chicago in 1950.

It stands for a democratic, secular Lithuania of small farmers: land for those who till it, cooperatives, rural schools, social insurance and a firm separation of church and state. Anti-Soviet but critical of clerical and nationalist dominance in the emigration, it holds the democratic left of exile politics. Its base is former teachers, cooperative organisers and farmers' sons scattered across North America.

19.name: Nacionalkomunistai
19.text:
The National Communists are the Lithuanians within the party and the Soviet establishment who want communism to wear a Lithuanian face. They take heart from Sniečkus's protection of native cadres and from the reclaiming of national history in literature, above all Justinas Marcinkevičius's 1968 verse drama 'Mindaugas', which made Lithuania's first king a stage hero. Planners, academics, editors and younger functionaries form their milieu.

They seek a Lithuania that is socialist but master of its own culture and economy: Lithuanian as the language of public life, control over immigration and investment, restoration of historic monuments and a stronger voice for Vilnius. They shun exiles and dissent and work through official channels. Their leverage lies in republican institutions, the Academy of Sciences, the Writers' Union and the press.

20.name: Lietuvių tautininkų sąjunga
20.text:
The Lithuanian Nationalist Union, the tautininkai, was the ruling party of Antanas Smetona's authoritarian regime from the coup of December 1926 to the Soviet occupation of 1940, and the only party permitted after 1936. Smetona died in exile in Cleveland in 1944, and his followers keep the movement alive in the United States through their own national league and the Cleveland weekly Dirva.

It stands for an integral nationalism built around the nation and a strong leader: discipline, patriotism, reverence for Smetona as 'Leader of the Nation' and suspicion of party politics. It rejects all contact with Soviet Lithuania and contests the Christian Democrats' dominance of exile institutions. Its leverage lies in veterans of the pre-war state apparatus and in a press that still shapes conservative émigré opinion.

21.name: Lietuvių aktyvistų frontas
21.text:
The Lithuanian Activist Front was founded in Berlin in November 1940 by Kazys Škirpa, the former envoy to Germany, to prepare an uprising against Soviet rule. In June 1941, as the Wehrmacht invaded, its insurgents seized Kaunas and proclaimed a Provisional Government, but the Germans dissolved the Front in September 1941. Its propaganda was openly antisemitic, and armed insurgents took part in the first massacres of Lithuania's Jews.

What remains is a network of ageing former activists around Škirpa, who lives in Washington and defends the uprising as a national act. Its creed is authoritarian and ethnic: a 'new Lithuania' purged of communists and Jews, a single national movement in place of parties and alignment with any power that fights Moscow. Discredited in the West, it has no organised following.

22.name: Lietuvos šaulių sąjunga išeivijoje
22.text:
The Lithuanian Riflemen's Union, founded in 1919 as a volunteer paramilitary force of patriotic citizens, was the backbone of national defence and youth training in independent Lithuania until the Soviet authorities dissolved it in 1940 and hunted its members. Riflemen who escaped to the West re-founded it in Chicago in March 1954, and it now has companies across the United States, Canada and Australia.

It upholds the ideal of the armed citizen: military discipline, patriotic education, marksmanship and readiness to restore Lithuanian statehood when the moment comes. Fiercely anti-communist and close to the nationalist wing of the emigration, it keeps the uniforms, banners and rituals of the pre-war union alive. Its leverage lies in discipline, symbolism and the memory of the riflemen who fought in the partisan war of 1944–53.

23.name: Haus Urach
23.text:
The House of Urach is the Catholic, morganatic branch of the royal house of Württemberg whose head, Wilhelm Karl, Duke of Urach, was elected King of Lithuania as Mindaugas II by the Council of Lithuania on 11 July 1918. The Council revoked the election that November as German power collapsed and the republic took shape; Wilhelm died in 1928, and the house is now headed by his son Karl Gero, Duke of Urach.

The claim survives as a cherished footnote among a few monarchist émigrés: a Catholic, constitutional crown for Lithuania, independent of both Germany and Russia and anchored in the memory of King Mindaugas and the Grand Duchy. The family itself pursues no restoration. Its leverage is purely symbolic, resting on the only royal election in modern Lithuanian history.
